page: Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is a virtual server belonging to the High Frequency Compute family. It features 4 shared vCPUs mapped to 2 physical Intel x86_64 cores with hyper-threading enabled. The system is configured with 16.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB per core. Local storage is bundled, consisting of a 384 GB NVMe SSD. No dedicated GPU is present. Network connectivity includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark results show average performance in single-core operations, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2411.16 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1471.0. However, because the CPU allocation is shared, multi-core scaling is limited, as evidenced by a weak Geekbench multi-core score of 4280.0 and a weak stress-ng multi-core score of 8740.87. Memory performance is highly asymmetrical: small-block cached read bandwidth is strong at 497.33 GB/sec, but large-block uncached read and write bandwidths fall into the bottom 25% at 35.47 GB/sec and 17.49 GB/sec respectively. Cryptographic and database operations also show weaker relative performance, with Passmark database operations scoring 2003.37 and Redis SET operations reaching 6.0 million operations per second.

Given its shared CPU architecture and budget-friendly positioning, this instance offers a cost-effective entry point for workloads requiring high-frequency single-core bursts and fast local NVMe storage without sustained multi-core demands. It is well-suited for lightweight web serving, development environments, basic text processing, and small-scale applications. It is less suitable for heavy multi-threaded compilation, large-scale database operations, or complex LLM inference, where its shared CPU and uncached memory bandwidth limitations would restrict throughput.

It is equipped with 16.0 GB of RAM and a bundled 384 GB NVMe SSD, but lacks a dedicated GPU. Performance benchmarks indicate average single-core capabilities, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2411.16, but multi-core and large-block memory bandwidth benchmarks fall into the lower percentiles due to the shared CPU allocation. This resource profile makes the server a cost-effective option for workloads that prioritize fast local storage and single-threaded burst performance over sustained multi-threaded compute.
